questions.question: The National Rice Research Institute is located at ________ in Odisha.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cuttack**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The National Rice Research Institute (NRRI) is located in **Cuttack, Odisha**.
 
• NRRI was established in the year 1946 and is one of the premier institutes under the **Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR).**
 
• The institute focuses on rice research and development, and plays a crucial role in advancing rice cultivation techniques in India.
 
• NRRI also works towards addressing challenges related to rice production, such as pest management, yield improvement, and climate resilience.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rice Research in India:**

 
 
• India is one of the largest producers of rice, and research plays a pivotal role in improving rice varieties and yields.
 
• Research institutes like NRRI contribute to the development of high-yielding and stress-tolerant rice varieties.
 
 
 
• **Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR):**
 
 
• ICAR is an autonomous organization under the Department of Agricultural Research and Education, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Government of India.
 
• It coordinates agricultural education and research in India and has numerous institutes dedicated to various aspects of agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Rice:**
 
 
• Rice is a staple food for a large portion of the global population, particularly in Asia.
 
• It is crucial for food security and provides essential nutrients and calories.
 
 
 
• **Climate Change and Rice Cultivation:**
 
 
• Climate change poses significant challenges to rice cultivation, including changes in rainfall patterns, temperature fluctuations, and increased frequency of extreme weather events.
 
• Research institutes like NRRI work on developing climate-resilient rice varieties to ensure sustainable production.

questions.question: In how many phases was the 2011 Census conducted in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Two**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 2011 Census of India was conducted in two distinct phases.
 
• The first phase, known as the House listing and Housing Census, took place from April to September 2010.
 
• The second phase, Population Enumeration, was conducted from 9th to 28th February 2011, with a revision round from 1st to 5th March 2011.
 
• The Census was carried out by the Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
• It was the 15th National Census of the country since 1872.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **House Listing Phase:**

 
 
• This phase involved the listing of all houses, whether occupied or vacant, and collecting information on the amenities available to the households.
 
• It also included a National Population Register (NPR) for the biometric details of residents.
 
 
 
• **Population Enumeration Phase:**
 
 
• This phase recorded demographic details of the individuals such as name, age, sex, religion, and occupation.
 
• Special provisions were made to include homeless populations and those living in institutions.
 
 
 
• **National Population Register (NPR):**
 
 
• The NPR was created to have a comprehensive identity database of residents.
 
• It includes demographic and biometric data of individuals.
 
 
 
• **Technology Use:**
 
 
• For the first time, the 2011 Census used modern technology like GIS and GPS for mapping and data collection.
 
• Data processing was done using advanced software to ensure accuracy and speed.

questions.question: _______ means avoiding imports of goods which could be produced in India.
questions.solution:

__
 
• Self-reliance refers to the ability of a country to produce essential goods and services domestically, minimizing dependency on imports.
 
• It aims to strengthen the economic independence of a nation by supporting local industries and reducing the trade deficit.
 
• India has emphasized self-reliance through initiatives like "Make in India," which encourages companies to manufacture their products within the country.
 
• Self-reliance is also linked to national security, as it ensures that critical supplies are available without dependency on foreign nations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atmanirbhar Bharat**:

 
 
• Launched by the Indian government in 2020, Atmanirbhar Bharat aims to make India a self-reliant nation.
 
• The initiative focuses on boosting local manufacturing, promoting local products, and reducing import reliance.
 
• It includes measures for various sectors, including agriculture, defense, and MSMEs (Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises).
 
 
 
• **Import Substitution**:
 
 
• This economic policy advocates replacing foreign imports with domestic production.
 
• It aims to reduce foreign dependency and improve local industry by providing incentives and protections.
 
 
 
• **Economic Growth**:
 
 
• Economic growth refers to an increase in the production of goods and services in an economy over a period of time.
 
• It is measured by the growth in Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
 
 
 
• **Modernisation**:
 
 
• Modernisation involves updating and improving infrastructure, technology, and processes.
 
• It aims to enhance efficiency, productivity, and competitiveness in the global market.

questions.question: What are the compounds in food that induce the growth or activity of beneficial gut microorganisms called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prebiotics**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Prebiotics are compounds in food that induce the growth or activity of beneficial microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
 
• They are typically non-digestible fibers that serve as food for probiotics, promoting a healthy gut microbiome.
 
• Common prebiotics include inulin, fructooligosaccharides (FOS), and galactooligosaccharides (GOS).
 
• Prebiotics are found in foods such as garlic, onions, bananas, and whole grains.
 
• They play a crucial role in maintaining digestive health and boosting the immune system.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Probiotics:**

 
 
• Live beneficial bacteria found in fermented foods and supplements.
 
• They help restore the natural balance of gut bacteria when it has been disrupted.
 
• Common probiotic foods include yogurt, kefir, sauerkraut, and kimchi.
 
 
 
• **Synbiotics:**
 
 
• Products that contain both prebiotics and probiotics.
 
• Aim to enhance the survival and colonization of beneficial bacteria in the gut.
 
• Examples include certain dietary supplements and functional foods.
 
 
 
• **Gut Microbiome:**
 
 
• Refers to the diverse community of microorganisms living in the digestive tracts of humans and other animals.
 
• Plays a critical role in digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.
 
• Imbalances in the gut microbiome are linked to various health issues including inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, and mental health disorders.
 
 
 
• **Dietary Fiber:**
 
 
• A type of carbohydrate that the body cannot digest.
 
• Promotes bowel regularity and helps prevent constipation.
 
• Found in foods such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes.

questions.question: Which of the following social reform organisations was established in Madras in 1864?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Veda Samaj**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Veda Samaj was established in Madras (now Chennai) in 1864.
 
• It was founded by Keshab Chandra Sen and later renamed as the Brahmo Samaj of South India.
 
• The organization aimed at promoting social reforms such as the abolition of caste distinctions and child marriage.
 
• The Veda Samaj was inspired by the principles of the Brahmo Samaj, advocating monotheism and rationalism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Brahmo Samaj:**

 
 
• Founded in 1828 by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in Calcutta (now Kolkata).
 
• It played a key role in the social and religious reform movements in India.
 
• Advocated for the abolition of practices like Sati and child marriage.
 
 
 
• **Arya Samaj:**
 
 
• Founded by Swami Dayananda Saraswati in 1875 in Bombay (now Mumbai).
 
• Promoted Vedic teachings and opposed idolatry and caste-based discrimination.
 
• Focused on education and social reform.
 
 
 
• **Prarthana Samaj:**
 
 
• Founded in 1867 in Bombay (now Mumbai) by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang.
 
• Focused on social reforms like widow remarriage and improving the status of women.
 
 
 
• **Social Reforms in 19th Century India:**
 
 
• 19th century India witnessed a wave of social reform movements aimed at eradicating social evils and promoting modernization.
 
• Leaders like Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Swami Dayananda Saraswati, and others played pivotal roles.
 
• These movements laid the foundation for subsequent reforms and the struggle for India's independence.

questions.question: The revenue raised by the central bank through printing of money is called ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Seigniorage**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Seigniorage** is the profit made by a central bank from issuing currency, especially the difference between the face value of coins or notes and their production costs.
 
• This economic term originates from the Old French word "seigneuriage," which referred to the right of the lord to coin money.
 
• Seigniorage serves as a source of revenue for governments, helping to finance various public expenditures without raising taxes.
 
• The concept is crucial in understanding how central banks manage monetary policy and control inflation.
 
• Seigniorage can also refer to the benefits reaped from the inflation tax, where the real value of currency held by the public decreases as inflation rises.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Inflation Tax**

 
 
• The inflation tax refers to the loss of purchasing power experienced by holders of cash and cash equivalents due to inflation.
 
• It acts as an implicit tax on holders of money, as the real value of their holdings decreases over time.
 
• Governments benefit from this as it reduces the real value of their debt.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy**
 
 
• Monetary policy involves the management of interest rates and the total supply of money in circulation, typically carried out by central banks.
 
• It aims to control inflation, manage employment levels, and ensure economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Fiat Currency**
 
 
• Fiat currency is government-issued currency that is not backed by a physical commodity like gold or silver.
 
• The value of fiat money is derived from the relationship between supply and demand and the stability of the issuing government.
 
 
 
• **Quantitative Easing**
 
 
• Quantitative easing (QE) is a monetary policy where a central bank buys government securities or other securities from the market to increase the money supply and encourage lending and investment.
 
• It is used to stimulate the economy when standard monetary policy has become ineffective.

questions.question: When several political parties join hands to form a government and exercise political power on the basis of a consensus programme agenda, it is called what?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Coalition government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A coalition government is formed when multiple political parties join hands to create a majority in the legislature.
 
• This type of government usually arises when no single party gains a sufficient number of seats to form a majority on its own.
 
• Coalition governments are based on a consensus programme agenda agreed upon by all the participating parties.
 
• Such a government requires constant negotiation and compromise among the member parties to maintain stability.
 
• Examples include the Indian National Democratic Alliance (NDA) and the United Progressive Alliance (UPA).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Majority Party Government**

 
 
• A majority party government is when a single political party wins more than half the seats in the legislature and forms the government independently.
 
• It usually results in a more stable and efficient administration as compared to coalition governments.
 
 
 
• **Presidential Government**
 
 
• This system features a president who serves as both the head of state and the head of government.
 
• It is characterized by a clear separation of powers between the executive and the legislature.
 
• Examples include the United States and Brazil.
 
 
 
• **One-Party System**
 
 
• In a one-party system, a single political party controls the government and other parties are either banned or allowed limited participation.
 
• It often leads to a lack of political pluralism and can be associated with authoritarian regimes.
 
• Examples include China and North Korea.
 
 
 
• **Consensus Programme Agenda**
 
 
• This refers to an agreed-upon set of policies and priorities that coalition parties commit to implementing together.
 
• It ensures that all coalition members have a stake in the government’s agenda, promoting cooperation and reducing conflicts.

questions.question: Who among the following Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi dancers received the Padma Vibhushan award in the year 2016?

questions.question: Who among the following fought the Mughal emperor Babur in 1527 at Khanwa?

__
 
• Rana Sanga, also known as Maharana Sangram Singh, was the ruler of Mewar in Rajasthan.
 
• He fought the Battle of Khanwa against the Mughal emperor Babur on March 16, 1527.
 
• The battle was significant as it marked the establishment of Mughal rule in India after defeating the Rajput confederacy.
 
• Rana Sanga's forces were ultimately defeated by Babur's well-organized and strategically superior army.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Babur's Strategy**: Babur used advanced artillery and tactics such as the Tulughma (dividing the army into smaller units) and Araba (using carts for defense) to defeat Rana Sanga.
 
• **Rajput Confederacy**: Rana Sanga led a confederacy of Rajput states and other allies against Babur, demonstrating a united front against the Mughal invasion.
 
• **Aftermath of the Battle**: The defeat at Khanwa weakened the Rajput resistance and paved the way for the Mughal Empire to consolidate its power in northern India.

• The Bardoli Satyagraha took place in the year **1928** in the Bardoli taluka in Gujarat.
 
• It was led by **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**, who earned the title of 'Sardar' due to his leadership in this movement.
 
• The movement was a response to the **increased land revenue assessment** by the British government.
 
• The peasants of Bardoli refused to pay the increased taxes and faced property confiscation, but they remained non-violent throughout the struggle.
 
• The movement gained national attention and was a significant event in the Indian independence struggle, leading to the eventual rollback of the tax hike.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel:**

 
 
• He was an Indian statesman and a senior leader of the Indian National Congress during the struggle for independence.
 
• He played a key role in the integration of the princely states into the Indian Union post-independence.
 
• Known as the 'Iron Man of India', he was instrumental in the success of the Bardoli Satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **Non-violent resistance:**
 
 
• A form of protest or resistance where participants do not use physical force.
 
• It was a cornerstone of the Indian independence movement, largely influenced by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
 
 
• **Land revenue system in British India:**
 
 
• The British imposed various land revenue systems like Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, and Mahalwari.
 
• These systems often led to increased taxes and exploitation of farmers.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Bardoli Satyagraha:**
 
 
• The success of the Bardoli Satyagraha inspired further movements and strengthened the resolve of the Indian populace against colonial rule.
 
• It also demonstrated the power of organized, non-violent resistance.

questions.question: In an ecosystem, which of the following is/are autotrophs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Plants**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Plants** are **autotrophs**, meaning they produce their own food using sunlight, carbon dioxide, and water through the process of photosynthesis.
 
• Autotrophs are also known as **primary producers** because they form the base of the food chain in an ecosystem.
 
• Photosynthesis in plants occurs in the chloroplasts, which contain the pigment **chlorophyll** that captures light energy.
 
• Through photosynthesis, plants convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose, which is used to fuel their growth and metabolism.
 
• Examples of other autotrophs include **algae** and some bacteria, but in the context of the question, plants are the correct option.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Autotrophs vs. Heterotrophs:**

 
 
• **Autotrophs** can synthesize their own food from inorganic substances, while **heterotrophs** obtain their food by consuming other organisms.
 
• Examples of heterotrophs include animals, fungi, and most bacteria.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Autotrophs:**
 
 
• Autotrophs are crucial for the survival of ecosystems as they produce organic matter that feeds heterotrophs.
 
• They also play a significant role in carbon fixation, helping to regulate the global carbon cycle.
 
 
 
• **Photosynthesis:**
 
 
• Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize foods with the help of chlorophyll.
 
• The general equation for photosynthesis is:

 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂.
 
 
 
• **Chlorophyll:**
 
 
• Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plants that absorbs light energy used in photosynthesis.
 
• There are several types of chlorophyll, but chlorophyll-a is the most common in plants.
 
 
 
• **Role of Light in Photosynthesis:**
 
 
• Light is a crucial component of photosynthesis as it provides the energy needed to drive the reactions that convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
 
• Plants absorb light primarily in the blue and red wavelengths and reflect green light, which is why they appear green.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India deals with the National Commission for Scheduled Castes?

__
 
• **Article 338** of the Constitution of India deals with the establishment of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC).
 
• The NCSC was reconstituted as a separate entity distinct from the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST) through the 89th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003.

• To advise on the planning process of socio-economic development of SCs.
 
• To present reports to the President on the working of these safeguards.
 
 
 
• **Composition of NCSC**:
 
 
• The NCSC consists of a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson, and three other members appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

questions.question: Which of the following international organisations was founded in 1995?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established on 1 January 1995.
 
• It succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), which had been in place since 1948.
 
• The WTO is the only global international organization dealing with the rules of trade between nations.
 
• Its main function is to ensure that trade flows as smoothly, predictably, and freely as possible.
 
• As of 2023, the WTO has 164 member countries, making it one of the largest international economic organizations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• GATT was a legal agreement minimizing barriers to international trade by eliminating or reducing quotas, tariffs, and subsidies while preserving significant regulations.
 
• It came into force on 1 January 1948 and was in place until it was replaced by the WTO.
 
 
 
• **WTO Ministerial Conference**
 
 
• The Ministerial Conference is the topmost decision-making body of the WTO and usually meets every two years.
 
• It brings together all members of the WTO, all of which are countries or customs unions.
 
 
 
• **Dispute Settlement Mechanism**
 
 
• The WTO provides a forum for negotiating agreements aimed at reducing obstacles to international trade and ensuring a level playing field for all its members.
 
• Its Dispute Settlement Body is crucial for resolving trade disputes between member governments.
 
 
 
• **Trade Policy Review Mechanism**
 
 
• This mechanism is designed to improve adherence by all members to the rules and disciplines made under the multilateral trade agreements.
 
• It serves as a means of monitoring and evaluating the trade policies and practices of member countries.

questions.question: What is epeirogenic process?

options.text: It involves the horizontal movement of the crustal plate.
This involves relatively little movement of water.
This involves relatively little movement of rocks.
It involves the uplift or folding of large portions of the Earth's crust.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It involves the uplift or folding of large portions of the Earth's crust.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Epeirogenic Process**

 
 
• The term "epeirogenic process" refers to the vertical movements of the Earth's crust that result in the formation of large-scale features such as plateaus, mountain ranges, and other landforms, primarily through processes like uplift or subsidence.
 
• This type of process typically affects vast regions of the Earth's surface and results in slow, widespread changes over long periods.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Characteristics:**

 
 
• **Vertical Movements: **Epeirogenic movements mainly involve vertical shifts in the Earth's crust, either raising or lowering large land areas.
 
• **Large Scale: **These movements affect extensive areas, often leading to the formation of extensive plateaus or broad mountain ranges.
 
• **Slow Process:** Epeirogenic movements occur slowly over millions of years and are typically less dramatic than tectonic (or orogenic) movements, which involve more localized, intense activity.
 
• **No Major Faults or Folds: **Unlike orogenic processes, epeirogenic movements do not typically cause large faults or folds but can result in more subtle deformations.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Epeirogenic Movements:**
 
 
• The uplift of the Colorado Plateau in the United States.
 
• The Siberian Plateau in Russia, which is a result of slow vertical movements.
 
• These processes are crucial in shaping the Earth's topography, but they are subtle and often go unnoticed compared to more active tectonic movements.

questions.question: The English novel ‘Heart of Darkness’ was written by which of the following authors?

• **Joseph Conrad** wrote the novel **'Heart of Darkness'**, which was first published in 1899 as a three-part series in Blackwood's Magazine.
 
• The novel is **set in Africa** and follows the journey of Charles Marlow, who travels up the Congo River in search of the enigmatic Kurtz.
 
• 'Heart of Darkness' is often regarded as a critique of European colonialism and the moral and ethical issues associated with it.
 
• Joseph Conrad's narrative style and use of a **frame story** technique are significant aspects of this work, influencing many subsequent writers and literary works.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Charles Marlow**: The protagonist of the novel, Marlow serves as Conrad's alter ego and recounts his journey into the Congo.
 
• **Kurtz**: A central character in 'Heart of Darkness', Kurtz is an ivory trader who has become a demigod among the native Africans but loses his humanity in the process.
 
• **Colonialism**: The novel explores the exploitation and brutality of European colonialism in Africa, highlighting the dehumanizing effects on both the colonizers and the colonized.
 
• **Frame Story**: Conrad employs a frame narrative, where the story is told by Marlow to his friends aboard a boat anchored on the River Thames, creating a story within a story.
 
• **Influence and Legacy**: 'Heart of Darkness' has influenced numerous works, including Francis Ford Coppola's film 'Apocalypse Now', which transposes the story to the Vietnam War era.

• **Allotropes**: Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, like graphite and diamond for carbon.
 
• **Stereoisomers**: Isomers that have the same molecular formula and connectivity but differ in the spatial arrangement of atoms.

questions.question: Which of the following writs are issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Prohibition and Certiorari**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Prohibition** is a writ issued by a superior court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent it from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting contrary to the rules of natural justice.
 
• **Certiorari** is a writ issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal either to transfer the matter for review or to quash the order of the lower court.
 
• Both **Prohibition** and **Certiorari** are issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies and not against administrative authorities, legislative bodies, or private individuals.
 
• The purpose of **Prohibition** is to stop the lower court or tribunal from continuing the proceedings in a particular case, while **Certiorari** is to ensure that the lower court's decision is reviewed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mandamus**: A writ issued to command a public official, government, or a lower court to perform a duty that they are legally obligated to complete.
 
• **Habeas Corpus**: A writ requiring a person under arrest to be brought before a judge or into court, ensuring the individual's release unless lawful grounds are shown for their detention.
 
• **Quo Warranto**: A writ issued to challenge the legality of a person's claim to a public office.
 
• **Judicial Bodies**: Entities that have the authority to adjudicate legal disputes and interpret laws, such as courts.
 
• **Quasi-Judicial Bodies**: Entities that have powers resembling those of a court of law and are responsible for adjudicating disputes, such as tribunals.

questions.question: Which are the most explosive of the earth’s volcanoes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Caldera**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Caldera** eruptions are the most explosive volcanic events on Earth.
 
• These eruptions are characterized by the collapse of the magma chamber, which leads to the formation of a large crater.

• **Prohibition**: A writ issued to lower courts or tribunals to prevent them from exceeding their jurisdiction.
 
• **Certiorari**: A writ issued to lower courts or tribunals to transfer a matter to a higher authority for review and re-examination.
 
• **Quo Warranto**: A writ used to challenge the legality of a person's claim to a public office.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements with respect to the limitations of the barter exchange system.

(i) Lack of standard of deferred payment

(ii) Sufficient double coincidence of wants

(iii) Lack of store of value

Choose the correct answer.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both (i) and (iii) are true**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The barter exchange system faces a significant limitation due to the **lack of a standard of deferred payment**, meaning future payments or credits can't be standardized.
 
• Another major limitation is the **lack of a store of value**, making it difficult to save wealth or transfer it over time.
 
• The system requires a **double coincidence of wants**, which means that two parties must have exactly what the other wants, making transactions cumbersome and less likely.
 
• The absence of a standardized value system complicates price setting and the valuation of goods and services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Double Coincidence of Wants:**

 
 
• This term refers to the situation where two parties each possess something the other wants, which is necessary for a barter exchange.
 
• It is a significant limitation as it makes finding a trading partner difficult.
 
 
 
• **Standard of Deferred Payment:**
 
 
• This refers to an accepted way of valuing debt or future payments, which is impossible in a barter system.
 
 
 
• **Store of Value:**
 
 
• A function of money that allows it to be saved and retrieved in the future, retaining its value over time.
 
• Barter systems lack this, making it difficult to save wealth.
 
 
 
• **Unit of Account:**
 
 
• A standard numerical monetary unit of measure that allows the value of goods and services to be compared.
 
• Barter systems do not provide a unit of account, complicating pricing and valuation.

questions.question: Aryabhatta is believed to be one of the greatest astronomers of the:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aryabhatta**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Aryabhatta was a prominent Indian mathematician and astronomer who lived during the Gupta period, around 476-550 CE.
 
• He is best known for his work "Aryabhatiya," which covers arithmetic, algebra, plane trigonometry, and spherical trigonometry, along with continued fractions, quadratic equations, sums of power series, and a table of sines.
 
• Aryabhatta's astronomical calculations included the Earth's circumference and the theory that the Earth rotates on its axis, thus explaining the apparent westward motion of stars.
 
• His calculations of the solar and lunar eclipses were remarkably accurate for his time.
 
• The Aryabhata satellite, India’s first satellite, was named in his honor and launched in 1975.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gupta Period:**

 
 
• The Gupta period is often referred to as the Golden Age of India due to significant achievements in arts, science, and literature.
 
• The period saw the flourishing of Sanskrit literature and the creation of important works like the plays of Kalidasa.
 
• In addition to Aryabhatta, other notable scholars from this period include Varahamihira and Brahmagupta.
 
• Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, and Chandragupta II were some of the prominent rulers of the Gupta dynasty.
 
 
 
• **Astronomical Contributions:**
 
 
• Aryabhatta's approximation of pi (π) was highly accurate, calculated as 3.1416.
 
• He introduced the concept of zero as a placeholder and the decimal system in Indian mathematics.
 
• Aryabhatta's work on the sidereal periods of the planets was crucial for the development of Indian astronomy.
 
 
 
• **Mathematical Achievements:**
 
 
• Aryabhatta's work laid the foundation for the development of trigonometry in India.
 
• He provided solutions to quadratic equations and worked on the summation of series.
 
• His work influenced later mathematicians in India and the Islamic world.
 
 
 
• **Aryabhatiya:**
 
 
• The text is divided into four sections: Gitikapada, Ganitapada, Kalakriyapada, and Golapada.
 
• It covers a wide range of mathematical and astronomical topics, including time calculations, planetary positions, and eclipses.
 
• The work was highly influential and was translated into Arabic, where it was studied by Islamic scholars.
